questions.q: Sabi's access tokens are JWTs that live 15 minutes. What makes it possible to end one of them immediately at logout?
questions.explain: A plain JWT is valid until it expires; nothing on the server remembers it. Binding it to a session gives the server a row it can delete. One cheap lookup per request buys instant logout, "sign out everywhere" and role changes that take effect at once.
options: JWTs can be deleted from the client
The token is encrypted, so the server can change the key
Each token carries its session id (sid), and auth.verifyToken refuses a token whose session no longer exists
Logout changes the signing secret

questions.q: A refresh token that was already used comes back. What does the platform do, and why?
questions.explain: A used refresh token should never come back. If it does, two parties have it. Ending all sessions forces both to log in again, and only the real user can. The demo showed the phone and the new laptop token dying too.
options: Returns the same new pair again, because the client probably retried
Refuses it and keeps everything else as it is
Refuses it and ends every session of that user, because someone copied the token and the server cannot tell whether the thief or the owner used it first
Locks the account for 15 minutes

questions.q: Why does createPgRevocationStore implement revokeIfNotRevoked as a single INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING?
questions.explain: "Check, then revoke" has a gap between two awaits. The unique key makes check and write one atomic step. Without the method, @zudojs/auth falls back to the racy pair, so always implement it in a real store.
options: Because PGlite has no transactions
So two copies of the same refresh token arriving together cannot both see "not revoked"; the primary key lets exactly one insert win
Because it is faster than a SELECT
Because the interface requires SQL

questions.q: Why does Sabi keep sessions in PostgreSQL instead of createMemorySessionStore()?
questions.explain: The memory store is fine for learning and single-process tests. In production, behind a load balancer, every server must see the same sessions: a database or Redis.
options: The memory store does not support expiry
Memory sessions vanish on restart and are not shared between servers, so a request on another server would find no session
The memory store stores tokens in clear text
PostgreSQL is faster than a Map

questions.q: A session has an idle timeout of 30 minutes and an absolute limit of 7 days. Ada uses the app every 10 minutes, day and night. When does her session end?
questions.explain: With only an idle timeout, a busy session (or a stolen one being used) lives forever. LEAST(now() + ttl, absolute_expires_at) in touch implements both clocks.
options: Never, because it is always active
After 30 minutes
After 7 days: every use pushes the idle deadline forward, but never past the absolute limit
After 15 minutes, when the access token expires

questions.q: Reset tokens are stored as SHA-256 hashes, while passwords use slow scrypt. Why is a fast hash acceptable for reset tokens?
questions.explain: Slow hashing protects low-entropy secrets from offline guessing. A random 32-byte token cannot be guessed in any number of tries, and a deterministic hash also lets you look the token up with WHERE token_hash = $1.
options: Reset tokens are not secret
SHA-256 is slower than scrypt
A reset token has 256 bits of randomness, so there is nothing to guess; slow hashing only helps against guessable inputs like human passwords
Because reset tokens expire, the hash does not matter

questions.q: Why does POST /v1/password-resets answer 202 with the same message for known and unknown e-mails?
questions.explain: A different answer for "no such account" is an enumeration oracle. The production concerns add the second half: the response time must not differ either, which is why the e-mail belongs on a queue.
options: Because the e-mail is sent later
So the endpoint cannot be used to find out which e-mail addresses have accounts
Because 404 is not allowed on POST
To save a database query

questions.q: The reset link is https://sabi.example/reset-password#token=…. What does putting the token after # achieve?
questions.explain: Query strings are logged by web servers and proxies and leak through the Referer header. The fragment stays in the browser. The token still travels, but only in a POST body to your API.
options: It encrypts the token
Browsers never send the fragment to a server, so the token stays out of server logs and Referer headers; the page's script reads it and POSTs it
It makes the link shorter
It makes the token expire when the tab closes

questions.q: Why does a successful password reset call auth.logoutAll(user)?
questions.explain: Refresh tokens live 7 days, and an attacker with a session can keep refreshing. Changing the password without ending sessions leaves the attacker inside.
options: To force the user to test the new password
Because the old tokens are signed with the old password
The usual reason for a reset is that someone else knows the password; their existing sessions must end with it
It does not matter; tokens expire in 15 minutes anyway

questions.q: confirm looks the token up before hashing the new password. What does that order protect?
questions.explain: An endpoint that runs expensive work before rejecting bad input can be used to burn CPU. Reject cheaply first. The conditional UPDATE afterwards still makes the token single-use if two requests race.
options: The token from being logged
The server: guessing tokens costs one cheap query each instead of a deliberately slow scrypt run
The password from being too short
Nothing; the order is only style

questions.q: Roles ride in the access token. When an admin makes Tunde a tutor, how does Tunde's access change?
questions.explain: Tokens cannot be edited, only replaced. Because they are session-bound, ending the sessions is how you replace them at once. The same works for demotions, which is the case that matters for security.
options: His current token is updated in place
After up to 15 minutes, when his token expires
The role change calls logoutAll for Tunde, his old tokens die at once, and his next login gets a token that says tutor
Only after the absolute session limit of 7 days

questions.q: Why does PUT /v1/users/:id/roles refuse an admin who tries to change their own roles?
questions.explain: Self-modification of privileges is a classic source of lockouts (and, the other way round, of escalation). Another admin, or a seed script on the server, handles it.
options: Admins have every permission already
So the last admin cannot demote themselves by accident and leave nobody able to assign roles
Because the token would become invalid
Because of the CHECK constraint

questions.q: A student registers with {"email": "…", "name": "…", "password": "…", "roles": ["admin"]}. Why does nothing happen with roles?
questions.explain: The client never chooses its own privileges. The schema is the allow-list, and the SQL hard-codes the default role. Incident 4 came from copying the body into the database.
options: The database rejects it
The registration schema has no roles field, so it is stripped, and the insert always adds the student role
The permission engine removes it
JSON.parse drops unknown keys

questions.q: Why are Kora identities stored by (provider, provider_id) and not by e-mail?
questions.explain: sub is the provider's permanent id for that person. E-mail is only used once, to decide whether to link or create, and only when verified.
options: E-mails are too long for a primary key
The provider's id is stable, while a person's e-mail can change at the provider; keying by e-mail would lose or mix up links
Because OAuth never returns an e-mail
For performance

questions.q: Kora returns email: "ada@example.com" with email_verified: false, and no identity is linked yet. What does Sabi do?
questions.explain: Anyone can type any e-mail into a new provider account. Linking or creating on an unverified address hands out other people's accounts, or blocks the real owner from registering.
options: Links it to Ada's account, because the e-mail matches
Creates a new account with that e-mail
Refuses the sign-in: an unverified e-mail proves nothing about who owns the inbox
Asks Kora again

questions.q: Mallory registered bola@example.com with a password before Bola joined. Bola now signs in with Kora (verified e-mail). What does Sabi do, and why?
questions.explain: This is the pre-account takeover from incident 3. Linking alone would leave Mallory with a working password on Bola's account. Evicting whoever set an unverified password closes it; verifying e-mails at registration keeps real owners from being surprised.
options: Refuses, because the e-mail is taken
Creates a second account for Bola
Links Kora to the account and leaves everything else unchanged
Links Kora to the account, removes its password and ends its sessions: Bola proved the inbox, and the unverified password may belong to someone else

questions.q: Where does Sabi keep the OAuth state and PKCE verifier between the start and the callback?
questions.explain: If the browser held the state itself, an attacker who controls the browser's inputs controls both sides of the comparison. On the server, it survives a callback that reaches another server, and deleting the row on use makes the callback single-use.
options: In a cookie holding both values
In the redirect URL
In the oauth_logins table, keyed by the hash of a random login id; the browser only holds the login id in an HttpOnly cookie
In localStorage

questions.q: The tests give @zudojs/auth-oauth a fetch that sends https://id.kora.example/… requests to the fake Kora on 127.0.0.1. Why not configure the endpoints as http://127.0.0.1:… directly?
questions.explain: A provider URL pointing at an internal address could turn your server into a tool for reaching internal services. The guard blocks it; the test routes the public name to the local fake instead of weakening the guard.
options: Because http is slower
The package's SSRF guard refuses provider URLs on loopback and private addresses, a protection you want in production
Because OAuth requires DNS
Because PKCE only works with https

questions.q: In accountFor, the lookup is SELECT … FROM users WHERE email = $1 FOR UPDATE. What does FOR UPDATE prevent?
questions.explain: The row lock serializes the two decisions. Where the row does not exist yet, the second insert then fails on the users or identities key instead of creating a duplicate.
options: Reading an old e-mail
Two simultaneous Kora logins for the same e-mail both deciding what to do with the same user row; the second waits for the first transaction
Deleting the user
SQL injection

questions.q: Why does Sabi's error handler copy headers from the thrown error?
questions.explain: @zudojs/http's built-in handling sends those headers; replacing it with your own handler means taking over that job. The lockout test checks the header, so this cannot silently break.
options: To add CORS headers
Some errors carry response headers, such as the lockout's Retry-After; a custom handler that builds its own response would otherwise drop them
To copy the request id
Because @zudojs/http requires it

questions.q: Logout reads the session id from the verified token's sid, not from the request body. What would go wrong with a body field?
questions.explain: Anything that decides whose data a request touches must come from verified credentials, not from what the client says.
options: Nothing, the body is validated
A caller could send someone else's session id and end their session
The body is not available in DELETE
Session ids are too long for JSON

questions.q: The auth service locks an e-mail after five wrong passwords. Which attack does that not stop, and what does?
questions.explain: A lockout counts per account, so an attacker spreading guesses across many accounts never trips it. A limit per client address, and in production shared counters across servers, covers that case.
options: Guessing many passwords for one account; the per-address rate limit
Trying one common password against thousands of accounts; the per-address rate limit on the login route
Stolen refresh tokens; the lockout
Replayed OAuth callbacks; the lockout

questions.q: Bola only ever signed in with Kora, so his password_hash is NULL. What happens when someone tries POST /v1/sessions with his e-mail and any password?
questions.explain: A missing credential must mean "no", never "anything goes". Bola can still set a password with a reset link if he wants one.
options: They are logged in, because there is no password to check
500, because the hash is NULL
401: checkPassword returns false for an account without a password, without hashing anything
400, because OAuth users cannot log in

questions.code:
import { serializeCookie } from "@zudojs/http";

questions.q: Write createLockout({ maxFailures, lockMs }) returning attempt(email, passwordOk, now). It returns "ok", "wrong" or "locked". After maxFailures consecutive wrong passwords the e-mail is locked for lockMs, even for the right password; a success resets the count. E-mails are compared after trimming and lower-casing. Print the results of the attempts below.
questions.explain: The third failure starts the lock, so even the right password at time 30 is refused. At 1030 the lock has passed and the success resets the count. Normalizing the e-mail stops an attacker from getting a fresh budget with ADA@example.com.
questions.expected: wrong wrong wrong locked ok wrong

questions.q: Write createRefresher() with issue(userId) (returns a new refresh token id and remembers it as unused) and refresh(tokenId). A known unused token is marked used and a new one is issued for the same user; a used one ends every session of its user (all their tokens become unusable) and returns "replay"; an unknown one returns "invalid". Use ids t1, t2, … Print the results below.
questions.explain: Replaying t1 ends everything Ada has, so the honest new token t3 and the phone's t2 are gone too. That is the price of not knowing who used the token first.
questions.expected:
t1 t2 t3
replay invalid invalid invalid

questions.q: Write createResetStore() with issue(userId, now) and use(token, now). issue returns a random token (use crypto.randomUUID()), keeps only its SHA-256 hex digest (use crypto.subtle.digest), deletes the user's older tokens, and makes it valid for 30 minutes (1 800 000 ms). use returns the user id once, then null. Print the results below.
questions.explain: The second request replaced the first link, the second link worked once, and a link at exactly 30 minutes is expired. Only digests are stored: a leak of rows gives away no working link.

questions.q: With @zudojs/permissions, build an engine where student has course:read, tutor inherits student, has course:create and may update a course only when isOwner("tutorId"), and admin inherits tutor and has course:* and user:assign-roles. Print one line per actor: can it update course { tutorId: 2 }, and can it assign roles?
questions.explain: Tutor 2 owns the course, tutor 3 does not. The admin's course:* allows every course action without the ownership rule, and only the admin may assign roles.
questions.expected:
1 [ 'student' ] false false
2 [ 'tutor' ] true false
3 [ 'tutor' ] false false
4 [ 'admin' ] true true

questions.q: Write confirmEmail(users, verification). verification is { userId, email } from a verification link. Mark the user's e-mail verified only if their current e-mail is still the one the link was sent to; return true or false. Print the results below.
questions.explain: User 2 changed their e-mail after the link was sent. Verifying anyway would mark an address as proven that nobody proved. Store the address with the token and compare it on use.
questions.expected:
true
false
ada@example.com: true, new@example.com: false

questions.q: Write assignRoles(actor, targetId, roles). Only an actor with role admin may assign; an admin may not change their own roles; every role must be one of student, tutor, admin; duplicates are removed and the result is sorted. Return { status, roles? } with 403, 400 or 200. Print the four results as JSON.
questions.explain: The permission check comes first, so a student learns nothing else. Self-changes and unknown roles are refused. In the platform, a successful change also ends the target's sessions.

questions.q: Write requestReset(email, users, outbox) for the reset request endpoint. It always returns { status: 202, message: "If the address has an account, a reset link is on its way." }, and only pushes { to } into outbox when an active user with that e-mail exists (compare trimmed and lower-cased). Print both results and the outbox.
questions.explain: A caller cannot tell the two answers apart. A deactivated account gets no link either, and still the same answer. In production, the e-mail goes on a queue so the timing does not differ either.
